entityDossier.whatItIs: The Air Technical Intelligence Center, formed in 1951 out of Air Materiel Command's T-2 intelligence organisation at Wright Field and resident at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. It was the United States' centre for the exploitation of foreign aerospace technology, the shop that processed the Operation Paperclip haul and took captured airframes apart. Every official American UFO project of the legacy era was hosted here: SIGN from 1948, GRUDGE from 1949 and Blue Book from 1952. It issued Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 on 5 May 1955 under Project 10073, Study No. 102-EL-55/2-79, and both editions of AFR 200-2 name it as the Air Force activity responsible for conducting analysis of information and evidence. It became the Foreign Technology Division in 1961 and later the National Air and Space Intelligence Center, which is still at the base.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The implicating fact is the assignment, not an allegation. The United States did not send unidentified flying objects to a science agency, to an academic body or to an air-defence command; it sent them to the organisation whose standing function was to answer one question about recovered hardware, which is what it is and how it works. That placement is usually reported as an administrative detail and is the structural point of this whole domain. The board also carries a Tier 2 custody link on the same ground: Howard McCoy ran AMC intelligence from 1945 to 1951, the organisation that received and exploited recovered foreign materiel and that hosted Project SIGN, so any 1947 recovery would have been processed at this address. And ATIC's own 1947-1951 T-2 intelligence files have never been subject to a comprehensive declassification review.
entityDossier.narrative:
Read the regulation rather than the folklore and the placement is explicit. AFR 200-2 of 26 August 1953, paragraph 4a, says that 'The Air Technical Intelligence Center (ATIC), Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, has been designated the Air Force activity responsible for conducting analysis of information and evidence.' The 1954 edition keeps the same terminal position, taking reports from base level through the Air Defense Command and the 4602d Air Intelligence Service Squadron and ending at ATIC.

One correction this board has had to make to its own corpus belongs here, because the mistake is easy and it repeats. The claim that AFR 200-2 routed reports to ATIC rather than to Blue Book is a category error. Project Blue Book was a project inside ATIC at Wright-Patterson; naming ATIC is naming Blue Book's host, and the 1953 regulation does not mention Blue Book at all in either edition.

The second thing the record establishes is that ATIC's analytical work was not confined to reports of things other people saw. TR-AC-47, the joint report on Project Silver Bug of 15 February 1955, carries the Air Technical Intelligence Center imprint on its title page, and its own conclusion asks for direct liaison between WADC and ATIC personnel. That is the same organisation, in the same year it published the largest statistical study of UFO reports the United States has ever produced, working with the Air Force's development command on a circular-planform aircraft.

entityDossier.denialPosture: ATIC is not recorded on this board issuing a denial of its own, and its D axis is 0. Its posture is structural rather than spoken: the regulation that named it the analysis authority is the same instrument that governed what could be said publicly, so the centre held the evidence and the parent service held the microphone. That division is worth stating plainly, because it means an absence of ATIC denials is not an absence of denial. The statements this board grades as directed denials in the legacy era are the Air Force's, and they are carried on the usaf node.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The National Security Agency, established on 4 November 1952 by a classified memorandum from President Truman, and like the National Reconnaissance Office an agency whose name the government preferred for decades not to confirm. Its place in this record is defined by one piece of litigation, Citizens Against UFO Secrecy v. National Security Agency, Civil Action No. 80-1562 in the District Court for the District of Columbia, and by two later events: its appearance among the contributing elements of ODNI's Preliminary Assessment of 25 June 2021, and its absence from the first statutory transfer of UAP records to the National Archives on 24 April 2025.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The operative fact is not that NSA won the case; it is what NSA conceded in order to win it. The Agency located a body of responsive material, withheld it in its entirety, and supported the withholding with a classified in camera affidavit executed by Eugene F. Yeates, Chief of the Office of Policy. The district court reviewed the full text ex parte, the D.C. Circuit affirmed in 1981 and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in 1982. What survives on the public record is therefore an adjudicated position that the Agency held UFO-related documents, that they were classified, and that their number and nature could not be described in open session. Forty years later ODNI named NSA among the elements contributing to the 2021 assessment, which places continuing signals-intelligence equity in the subject. Four years after that, NSA transferred nothing to the National Archives collection built for it.
entityDossier.narrative:
The three dated events read as one posture held across four decades, and each is a document rather than an allegation.

In 1980 the Agency answered a FOIA suit by conceding that responsive material existed and refusing to characterise it. The Yeates affidavit is the instrument by which a United States intelligence agency established in court that it held UFO material it could not describe publicly, and the public version of that affidavit was released only in heavily redacted form. On this board the resulting edge is graded a directed denial with NSA named as its issuer, because a refusal to describe is a dated, signed, attributable act by the refuser.

In 2021 ODNI's Preliminary Assessment listed NSA among the contributing elements, which is the government saying in its own publication that NSA collection produces UAP-relevant reporting. In 2025 the National Archives announced the first transfer under the statutory UAP records scheme and named only ODNI, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, the FAA and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. An agency with documented equity in the subject produced nothing, and the board carries that null return as the second directed denial on this node.

The Agency's own declassified collection contains one document worth naming for a different reason. It assesses the June 1978 GEPAN report and says that GEPAN's methods make 'the bulk of the Condon Report seem very poor by comparison'. That is a signals agency, in an internal assessment, grading the United States government's own public explanation as the weaker piece of work.

entityDossier.denialPosture: Two directed denials are recorded on this node and both are refusals to describe rather than assertions that nothing exists. In court the Agency said it had located responsive material and would not characterise it, and won on a showing no member of the public has seen. In 2025 it returned nothing to a statutory records collection built for exactly this subject, while four other bodies returned something. Neither event is NSA saying UAP are not real; both are NSA saying the question of what it holds is not answerable in the open. That is the more informative posture of the two, because it is falsifiable in principle and has never been falsified in practice.

entityDossier.whatItIs: Executive Order 13526, Classified National Security Information, signed on 29 December 2009 and published at 75 FR 707. It is the operative classification order and it is where special access programs come from. Section 4.3(a) restricts creation of a SAP to six officials or their principal deputies, the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and Homeland Security, the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence, and assigns intelligence SAPs to the DNI. Section 4.3(b) sets the internal rules: numbers kept at an absolute minimum, an accounting system in each agency, annual review, a briefing to the National Security Advisor on request, and access for the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office that the agency head may narrow. Section 4.3(c) subordinates the section to 10 U.S.C. 119, and section 6.2(a) subordinates the order to the Atomic Energy Act for Restricted Data.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Creation is executive and unilateral; reporting is statutory and comes afterward. Congress has never legislated over the authority to establish a special access program, so the six creating officials can stand one up with no statutory basis at all and 10 U.S.C. 119 only tells them what to report once it exists. The order is therefore the instrument that makes the central structural claim on this board possible rather than merely alleged, and it is the instrument agencies cite when they refuse to answer: two FOIA refusals carried here rest on it, USNORTHCOM in 2013 at section 1.4c and the Space Force in 2023 at section 1.1(a).
entityDossier.narrative:
The provision that matters most is the one that reads like housekeeping. Section 4.3(b)(3) grants the Director of ISOO access to special access programs and in the same breath says that 'An agency head may limit access to a special access program to the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.' The executive branch's own oversight body for the entire classification system can lawfully be reduced to a single individual, at the discretion of the person being overseen.

That is one of three narrowings, and the board's reading is that they are independent of each other. 10 U.S.C. 119(e) reduces the congressional readership of a waived SAP to twelve members. Section 4.3(b)(3) can reduce ISOO to one person. 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) relieves the Director of the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency of industrial-security oversight on a carve-out. Congressional, executive and industrial-security oversight are each narrowed by a different authority, so closing any one of them would leave the other two intact.

The order also contains the provisions a whistleblower would reach for, and they have no teeth inside the order itself. Section 1.7(a) forbids classification to conceal violations of law, inefficiency or administrative error, to prevent embarrassment, to restrain competition or to delay release of information that does not require protection; section 1.7(b) forbids classifying basic scientific research not clearly related to national security. Neither carries an enforcement mechanism in the text. The only channels are the section 5.3 appeal process and the intelligence-community whistleblower statutes.

entityDossier.denialPosture: An executive order does not deny; it is the instrument cited in denials, which is a different and more useful thing to be able to show. Two refusals on this board rest on it directly: USNORTHCOM's FOIA response in case FY14-19NOV2013-07, citing section 1.4c, and the Space Force position reported in December 2023 citing section 1.1(a). Both concern fastwalker and slowwalker material, both are exemption claims rather than assertions of non-existence, and both trace to the same document. The order's own section 1.7 makes several of the motives a reader might suspect impermissible on the face of the text, and supplies no way to test whether they were present.
connections: Sec. 4.3(c) subordinates the order to usc-10-119, which reports on the programmes the order creates.
All of the sap-taxonomy, acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived, operates below the section 4.3(a) grant.
Grants and simultaneously conditions isoo access to special access programs.
icd-906 section B.1 is the DNI's exercise of the section 4.3 authority for intelligence programmes.
ndaa-fy2024-7606 requires a personnel census from each head of an agency authorised to establish a SAP by this order.
Sec. 6.2(a) leaves Restricted Data, the category carried forward from the atomic-energy-act-1946, outside the order's reach.
Cited in both FOIA refusals recorded on defense-support-program, at sec. 1.4c in 2013 and sec. 1.1(a) in 2023.
openQuestions: How many special access programs exist is not established by anything on this board. The order requires each agency to keep an accounting system; no aggregate from one has been located.

Whether the President has ever exercised the 'unless otherwise authorized by the President' clause in sec. 4.3(a), or directed that ISOO be denied access to a specific programme, is not established. The board holds no document either way.
The annual reviews required by sec. 4.3(b)(4) and the on-request briefings under (b)(5) produce records by implication. None has been located, and no request for them is logged here.

entityDossier.whatItIs: Sandia National Laboratories, a Department of Energy federally funded research and development centre in Albuquerque, administered by National Technology and Engineering Solutions of Sandia, LLC since 1 May 2017. It is the largest FFRDC in the United States by funding, at approximately 4,584.0 million dollars in FY2024, and it sits adjacent to Kirtland Air Force Base, the installation that contains the Manzano Weapons Storage Area and Coyote Canyon.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The geography does most of the work, and it puts Sandia on this board twice over. In 1948 and 1949 the green fireballs that triggered the Los Alamos conference and Project Twinkle were concentrated over the atomic weapons installations, Los Alamos and Sandia among them. In August 1980 the best-documented American military UFO incident of the Cold War occurred on the adjoining base, and a Sandia security guard is a reporting party in the resulting Air Force Office of Special Investigations file. Thirty years later, three Sandia staff members were among the five outside reviewers of the FY09 AAWSAP technical reports, which is a DOE weapons laboratory peer-reviewing the physics portfolio of a Defense Intelligence Agency programme. The laboratory also appears in the custody record of an earlier document: the distribution list of AFSWC TR-59-39 sends a copy to the President of Sandia Corporation, attention Document Control Division.
entityDossier.narrative:
The 1980 file is the one to read. AFOSI Special Agent Richard C. Doty's complaint form of 9 September 1980, District File No. 8017D93-0/29, records that three members of the 1608 Security Police Squadron, SSgt Stephen Ferenz, ATC Martin W. Rist and AMN Anthony D. Frazier, observed a bright light near the Manzano restricted test range on the night of 8 August 1980 that made stop-and-go manoeuvres, landed in Coyote Canyon and departed vertically at high speed. The same file records a Sandia security guard observing a round disc-shaped object near an alarmed structure at about 00:20 on 9 August, his radio malfunctioning during the encounter.

What makes the file structurally interesting rather than merely anecdotal is that a contractor-operated national laboratory, an Air Force counterintelligence office and a nuclear weapons storage site all appear in one anomalous-object document. What makes it uncomfortable is what the same office and the same agent did next. Doty was the conduit for fabricated material supplied to Paul Bennewitz, the Albuquerque physicist whose company Thunder Scientific operated adjacent to Kirtland and who had licensed sensor technology from Sandia in 1966; the operation ended in Bennewitz's psychiatric collapse. The board grades that Tier 2 and attributes it to AFOSI, not to the laboratory.

The 2009 material is a different register and is worth keeping separate from the 1980 material. DIA memo U-429-09-DWO-IM of 30 October 2009 records the outside review of the AAWSAP deliverables, with three of the five reviewers from Sandia, and DIA recorded the reviews as positive. The board's reading of the timing is that DIA sought institutional cover for a portfolio it expected to have to defend, which it did five weeks later, and that reading is graded Tier 3 because it is an inference from sequence rather than anything the memo says.

That absence should be read carefully rather than charitably: the laboratory appears in the 1980 file as a reporting party, not as a respondent, and nothing here shows it was ever asked to account for what its guard saw. The deception in this story belongs to the Air Force counterintelligence office on the adjoining base, and the board keeps the attribution where the documents put it. What Sandia has not done, on any record held here, is say anything at all about August 1980.

entityDossier.whatItIs: AFSWC-TR-59-39, TR 59-39 Vol I, A Study of Lunar Research Flights, dated 19 June 1959 and issued by Headquarters Air Force Special Weapons Center, Air Research and Development Command, Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. It was written by L. Reiffel of the Armour Research Foundation at the Illinois Institute of Technology under Project Number 5776-57853 and Contract AF 29(601)-1164, with contributions from eleven others including C. E. Sagan. The copy read for this board is the Defense Documentation Center copy, AD 425380, read in full from the OCR text of the DTIC mirror.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: It is carried here as an instrument rather than as an anecdote. A dated federal record shows an Air Force laboratory paying a university research foundation to work out what could be learned from detonating a nuclear weapon on or near the Moon, and saying in its own introduction that one of the three motivations was political demonstration. The distribution list is the part with the most value to this board: it documents who in the nuclear weapons complex received a copy, which makes the report a custody record as well as a research study. Copies went to ARPA at the Pentagon, to the Atomic Energy Commission's technical reports library for the Division of Military Application, to Sandia Corporation's document control division, to Los Alamos, to Lawrence Radiation Laboratory and to WADD at Wright-Patterson.
entityDossier.narrative:
The document says the political part out loud. Chapter I: 'The motivation for such a detonation is clearly threefold: scientific, military and political... Obviously, however, specific positive effects would accrue to the nation first performing such a feat as a demonstration of advanced technological capability. It is also certain that, unless the climate of world opinion were well-prepared in advance, a considerable negative reaction could be stimulated.' The abstract is narrower and more technical, offering space environment investigation, detection of nuclear device testing and weapons capability in space as the military aspect.

Three corrections this node forces on the wider corpus are the reason it is worth having. The string 'A119' appears nowhere in the report; the document identifies itself only by report number and contract. The date is 19 June 1959, not 1958 and not May 1959. And the claim that the study was denied and then declassified after four decades of maintained non-existence is not established by the copy read here: it carries UNCLASSIFIED markings on its cover pages, its title is expressly marked '(Unclassified Title)', and no declassification stamp, downgrading instruction or distribution limitation appears in the OCR. Whatever the classification history was, this copy does not carry it.

The Sagan question is answered only as far as the paper goes. C. E. Sagan is on the contributor list on the report page, and the appendix separately places C. Sagan on the National Academy of Sciences WESTEX group and on the Armed Forces National Research Council Panel on Extraterrestrial Life. The document says nothing whatever about his security clearance, and the fellowship-application story that usually travels with this report concerns a different document that has not been opened here.

entityDossier.denialPosture: No denial attaches to this document on this board, and the popular framing that one should is the thing the record refuses. The claim usually made about it, that its existence was maintained as non-existent for four decades before a forced declassification, is not gradeable from the copy read: the DDC copy carries UNCLASSIFIED markings, an expressly unclassified title, and no declassification stamp, downgrading instruction or distribution limitation anywhere in the OCR. That is not a finding that the study was never withheld. It is a finding that this board holds no document establishing that it was, which is a different sentence and the only one the record supports.

openQuestions: The classification history of the study is not established. The DDC copy read here carries no declassification stamp or downgrading instruction, so whether an earlier copy was classified, and at what level, is unknown from this board.
The record here is Volume I. The board holds nothing on any further volume and has not established whether one exists.
The 1959 fellowship application in which the work is said to have been disclosed has not been opened. Nothing about it is in this report and no claim on this board rests on it.
Whether the copies sent to Sandia, Los Alamos, Lawrence Radiation Laboratory, ARPA and WADD survive in those institutions' records has not been tested by any request logged here.

entityDossier.whatItIs: United States Patent 10,144,532, 'Craft using an inertial mass reduction device', application 15/141,270, filed 28 April 2016 from the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division and granted 4 December 2018, assigned to 'The United States of America as represented by the Secretary of the Navy' under Navy docket PAX 205. The examiner was Philip J. Bonzell, supervised by Timothy Collins; the application moved from Art Unit 3644 to Art Unit 3642 mid-prosecution without changing examiner. The patent expired on 9 January 2023 for non-payment of the first maintenance fee under 37 CFR 1.362.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: It is the control case for the patents tab. A Navy-assigned propulsion filing that did issue is what makes an absence elsewhere in the patent record a legal artefact of the Invention Secrecy Act rather than evidence that nothing exists. It is also the filing that produced the public controversy, and the file wrapper contradicts the story most often told about it. The secondary accounts say the application was rejected and then granted after the Naval Aviation Enterprise's chief technology officer asserted operability and invoked Chinese development of comparable technology. The wrapper shows the examiner refusing that argument in writing, and shows the grant arriving through a formal appeal rather than a letter.
entityDossier.narrative:
The prosecution record is unusually explicit for a document of this kind, and it is worth following in order. Non-final rejection 28 November 2017. A telephonic examiner interview on 17 January 2018 at which, in the record's words, 'no agreement was reached'. Final rejection 30 March 2018. A response after final on 24 May 2018 carrying a declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 signed by Dr James Sheehy on 11 May 2018. Notice of Appeal 21 June 2018, on form PTO/AIA/33, an 800 dollar fee against deposit account 600508. Advisory Action 11 July 2018 refusing to allow. Appeal Brief 21 August 2018, re-filing the same 11 May declaration in its Evidence Appendix rather than a second one. Reasons for Allowance 24 October 2018, Notice of Allowance 31 October, grant 4 December. The examiner allowed the application before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board ever ruled.

The examiner quantified his objection rather than gesturing at it. Polarising a quantum vacuum as claimed 'would take 10^9 teslas and 10^18V/m', which 'are not feasible with current technology', and: 'The largest magnetic field ever created is 10^3 teslas and a neutron star is 10^6 teslas so how are you using a microwave emitter that produces a magnetic field that is three orders of magnitude greater than a neutron star?' The same passage repeats verbatim in the final rejection. He also rejected the physical premise in terms, writing that there is no such thing as a repulsive electromagnetic energy field and that electromagnetism can be repulsive in certain circumstances but there is no blanket field that repels everything.

On the argument the secondary accounts credit with winning the patent, the wrapper is unambiguous: 'With respect to third argument that China is already investing significantly in this area, this has nothing to do with what is patentable. If anyone else filed this Application they would receive the same rejection.' Peer review fared no better. On the AIAA and SAE presentations the examiner wrote that presentation and committee review 'does not equate to the device being patentable', and that 'Presenting math at a conference doesn't prove anything physical.'

What was eventually granted is narrow. Claim 1 is the only independent claim and recites an inner resonant cavity wall, an outer resonant cavity wall and microwave emitters creating high frequency electromagnetic waves that vibrate the outer wall in an accelerated mode and create a local polarized vacuum outside it. There are four claims in total. Five years later the Navy stopped paying for it.

entityDossier.denialPosture: The denial on this node runs in the unusual direction. The Navy did not deny anything about this filing; a federal examiner denied, on the record and in quantified terms, that the claimed effect is physically achievable, and did so twice before the applicant appealed. That is the only adjudicated technical opinion this board holds on any of the Pais filings, and it is negative. Two further things follow, and both matter for how the node should be read. The allowance that eventually issued came from the same examiner rather than from the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, so no appellate body has ever endorsed the disclosure. And the board's own edge from this patent to the five observables is graded Tier 2 and describes what the briefing claims the device would deliver, not a capability anyone has demonstrated.
connections: Arises from pax-205-disclosure, the internal Navy briefing carrying case number PAX 205.
salvatore-pais is the named inventor; us-navy is the assignee of record.
PAX 205 slide 5 says the IMRD enables pais-patent-hfgw, the gravitational wave generator, through the Gertsenshtein Effect.
The control case against invention-secrecy-act: a Navy propulsion patent that did issue.
Tier 2 link to five-observables as the mechanism the briefing offers for four of the mapped observables.
openQuestions: Whether the Navy's failure to pay the first maintenance fee was a decision or an oversight is not established. Nothing on this board explains the expiry.
Whether the Notice of Appeal was ever docketed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board is not established. The examiner allowed the application first, so no PTAB decision exists to read.

The node's own description still says the correspondence asserting operability has not been obtained for this board, while its claims cite the Sheehy letter of 15 December 2017 and the declaration of 11 May 2018 as transcribed under research/patents/wrapper/. The description is behind the claims and should be reconciled.
No test data, experimental result or hardware associated with the device has been located. The board holds the paper record of the filing and nothing else.
